newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX cuts clearing fees to boost Brent liquidity.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX cuts clearing fees to boost Brent liquidity.

text.p: The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) said on Friday it has cut clearing fees and waived booth rental charges since August 1 to boost liquidity on its Brent futures contract.
SIMEX has cut clearing fees on trades by 50 U.S cents per contract lot, or per 1,000 barrels, to 10 cents, a SIMEX spokesman said.
In addition, between August 1 and January 31 1997, SIMEX corporate members who bring in customer orders will be credited 50 cents per contract on Brent clearing fees, the spokesman told Reuters.
This clearing fee may be used to off set clearing fees payable by customers of corporate members on their trades in the Brent contract after January 31, 1997, he said.
The exchange is also waiving booth rentals for a maximum of two booths each for one year from 1 August 1996.
The spokeman told Reuters a single booth could cost up to Singapore $500 per month.
SIMEX introduced the incentives to boost liquidity of the Brent contract, he said.
Despite the incentives, SIMEX trading volumes in August registered a total of 3,480 lots, down from July's 3,786.
Brokers in Singapore said most traders preferred to wait until after London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) opens to provide market direction before trading.
They said this limited the activities on SIMEX to the last hour of trading as "trades only begin after about four o'clock in Singapore and the exchange closes at around five o'clock."

SIMEX launched the Brent-crude futures contract in June 1995 under a mutual offset system agreement with the IPE that allows the Brent contract to be traded for the 18 hours of combined trading of the two exchanges.
SIMEX is currently gathering feedback on the type of contract that would best suit the energy industry, industry sources said.
SIMEX launched a Dubai contract in June 20 and delisted it on June 31, 1992. It also launched a gasoil contract in 1991 but delisted it in 1993.
